title: The Studio That Never Travelled: Paris, Rome, and the Gods Shipped to Recoleta and Manhattan
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, the old eleventh arrondissement: the birth
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested by the French sources. The place is a district that no longer exists: the old eleventh was abolished by the law of 16 June 1859, effective 1 January 1860, and comprised the quartiers du Palais de Justice, de l'École de médecine, de la Sorbonne and du Luxembourg. The coordinate is a centroid of those quarters, not an address; no address is recorded anywhere reachable
stops.campa: A son is born into a Paris that is about to be redrawn. The old eleventh arrondissement runs from the Sorbonne to the Luxembourg and takes in the western tip of the Île de la Cité; a law passed when the boy is ten wipes it off the map, and before his twelfth birthday the district he was born in has ceased to exist. No street survives in the record, no house number, only the name of a quarter that outlived its own numbering by nothing at all. He will spend ninety years within a few kilometres of it, and die in the sixth arrondissement, on ground the old district used to cover.
suggested_refs: The ancien 11e arrondissement de Paris, abolished 1 January 1860

stops.name: École des beaux-arts, rue Bonaparte: the atelier of Cavelier
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The sources name Jules Cavelier as his master and the school as his training, but give no year of entry; 1866 is a placeholder set in the years before the 1872 prize. The coordinate is the school's rue Bonaparte entrance, the pin used elsewhere for this address
stops.campa: He enters the school on the rue Bonaparte and works under Jules Cavelier, a sculptor of the correct antique line, in the doctrine the Institut has enforced since before either of them was born: the figure built from the living model, the subject taken from Homer or from the Republic. The school ranks its pupils, and the ranking follows them out of the door. The commissions that reach him later, a porcelain works to run and a railway terminal in Manhattan to crown, all come through the system he is entering now, and he will end his life administering it.
suggested_refs: Jules Cavelier (1814-1894), his master at the École des beaux-arts

stops.name: École des beaux-arts: the Prix de Rome for Ajax
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested. The concours was judged in the summer, but no source consulted gives a month or a day, so the date defaults to 1 January
stops.campa: The great prize of the school goes to his 'Ajax bravant les Dieux et foudroyé': Ajax defying the gods and struck by lightning, a man burned off his rock for boasting that he could survive without the gods' consent, modelled in plaster by a candidate of twenty-three. The prize carries board and lodging in Italy at the Republic's expense, and it marks its winner for state commissions for decades afterwards. He takes up the lodging in Rome the following year.
suggested_refs: 'Ajax bravant les Dieux et foudroyé', Prix de Rome de sculpture, 1872

stops.name: Villa Médicis, Rome: the pensionnaire years
stops.date_confidence: the residency 1873-1876 is attested by the French sources and by Wikidata; no arrival date is given, and the day here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Above the Spanish Steps, in the villa the French Academy has held since Louis XIV, he takes his place among the pensionnaires: three years of drawing antique fragments and sending the required work north each year for the Institut to judge from Paris. The residents are laureates living under one roof and competing with one another, and the judging never stops. Which torso he copied, which frieze he drew, is not recorded in anything reachable. He goes home in 1876 with the manner he will keep for sixty years.
suggested_refs: The Académie de France à Rome at the Villa Médicis

stops.name: Rome: a small bronze called Standing Cupid
stops.date_confidence: the English article gives the year 1875 and nothing more. The work appears in no French list of his works, and the place tag attached to it there, Paris, is impossible for a man resident in Rome from 1873 to 1876; it is pinned at the villa on that ground, and both the attribution and the location are held loosely
stops.campa: A small bronze, a standing Cupid, is credited to this year and corroborated nowhere. It is the size of an ornament, cast rather than cut, an object made for a room and not for a square. The stone gods he will one day send to New York stand fifteen metres high; this one fits on a shelf. Bronzes of the domestic scale keep coming out of his studio for decades, cast by the Thiébaut Frères foundry and sold by the piece. They outlive in private houses whole monuments of his that were pulled down at the close of a fair.
suggested_refs: Thiébaut Frères, the Paris foundry that cast his small bronzes

stops.name: Paris: the studio after Rome
stops.date_confidence: the year of return is attested; the studio is a reconstruction. No address for any Coutan atelier appears in the sources consulted, and the coordinate is the Montparnasse and Plaisance quarter where sculptors of his generation clustered near the foundries. It is a guess at a neighbourhood, not a located building
stops.campa: He comes back from Italy into a city with an appetite for allegory. The Third Republic is filling its squares, bridges, ministries and museums with figures of Peace, Science, Labour and France, and it buys them through the Salon: one plaster judged each spring, one bronze cast if the judgment is good. He is twenty-seven and carries the Institut's stamp. Where he sets up his benches is written down nowhere that survives: no address for any Coutan atelier appears in the record, at any date, across sixty years of working life.
suggested_refs: The sculptors' quarter of Montparnasse and Plaisance in the 1870s
sources: reconstruction from the career pattern; no atelier address in fr.wikipedia or en.wikipedia

stops.name: Paris: the marriage to Suzanne Émilie Desbeaux
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested through Wikidata's citation of French biographical records; no month, day, parish or mairie is recorded. The coordinate is central Paris only and locates nothing
stops.campa: He marries Suzanne Émilie Desbeaux, sister of the writer Émile Desbeaux. Nothing else of the wedding survives: no church, no witnesses, no street, not even a month. The decade the marriage opens is the decorated one, the ribbon of a chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in July 1885, the gold medal of the exposition of 1889, the officer's promotion that same July. All of that is on file to the day. The marriage is two names and a year, and the wife appears in the record only as somebody's sister.
suggested_refs: Émile Desbeaux, writer, his brother-in-law
sources: Wikidata Q3183964, citing French biographical records

stops.name: Square d'Anvers, Paris: La Paix armée
stops.date_confidence: the French article on the parc Montsouris dates the making to 1888 and states the statue was conceived for the column of the square d'Anvers; it was removed in 1968 and set up in Montsouris only in 1984. The stop is pinned at the square it was made for. Any account placing it in the parc Montsouris in 1887 describes an event that did not happen
stops.campa: Armed Peace: a figure cut for the column of the square d'Anvers, at the foot of Montmartre, in a Republic that has not stopped counting the cost of 1870 and cannot yet say the word peace without an adjective. She stands over a public garden where the children of the ninth arrondissement play. In 1968 she is taken down, and sixteen years after that she is set up again on the far side of the city, in the parc Montsouris, which is where anyone looking for her now will find her, a long way from the column she was cut to crown.
suggested_refs: 'La Paix armée', square d'Anvers, later parc Montsouris

stops.name: Champ de Mars, Paris: the Fountain of Progress
stops.date_confidence: the year of the exposition is attested and the fountain is attested as his; no date is recorded for its unveiling. The gold medal and the promotion to officer of the Légion d'honneur, dated 13 July 1889, belong to the same summer and are folded into this stop
stops.campa: Under the new iron tower, on the fairground of the Exposition Universelle, his fountain group stands: France carrying the torch of civilisation, catalogued also as the Fountain of Progress. It is the register the fair requires of everyone on the field, Progress, Electricity, Empire, each given a woman's body and a raised arm. It wins him the gold medal, and in July the rosette of an officer of the Légion d'honneur. The fair is dismantled at the end of the season and the fountain goes down with it. The medal survives. The water does not.
suggested_refs: 'La France apportant le flambeau de la civilisation', Exposition Universelle, 1889

stops.name: Cimetière du Montparnasse: the Herbette tomb
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The French works list gives the sculpture on the Herbette family tomb with no date and no mention of a Salon; the year 1890 and the claim of a Salon showing come from elsewhere and are not corroborated. The coordinate is the centre of the cemetery, not the plot
stops.campa: Among the dense nineteenth-century rows he cuts the sculpture on the tomb of the Herbette family: a private commission in a career of public ones, with no Republic behind it and no jury, one household's grief handled by the hand that also carves states. The stone is still there, signed, in an avenue where almost nothing is read any more. Sculptors of his rank take work of this kind steadily between the great commissions, and the biographies give each of them a single line.
suggested_refs: The Herbette family tomb, cimetière du Montparnasse

stops.name: Bibliothèque nationale, site Richelieu: Le Manuscrit
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by the French works list; no month or day is given
stops.campa: In marble, for the library that has stood on this ground since the eighteenth century, he cuts an allegory called The Manuscript: the written word given a body, on a building whose only business is keeping the written word. The Republic decorates its institutions by one rule everywhere, one allegory to a discipline, one relief to a commission, and the sculptors of the Institut divide the disciplines among themselves. He takes the manuscript. In the same year the state hands him a factory to run.
suggested_refs: 'Le Manuscrit', marble, Bibliothèque nationale de France, site Richelieu

stops.name: Manufacture nationale de Sèvres: director of art works
stops.date_confidence: the term 1891-1894 is attested by the French sources and Wikidata; no month is given for the appointment or for the resignation. The coordinate is the manufacture's own, 48 degrees 49 minutes 43 seconds north, 2 degrees 13 minutes 21 seconds east
stops.campa: The state porcelain works, on the Seine at the edge of the Saint-Cloud park, has supplied the tables of kings and of republics since the eighteenth century. He is named director of its art works, and for three years the sculpting is other men's: he approves designs and oversees modellers, running a factory where French taste is argued out in glaze at the ministry's expense. In 1894 he gives it up for a chair at the school that trained him, and never administers anything again except an academy.
suggested_refs: The Manufacture nationale de Sèvres under the Third Republic

stops.name: Poitiers, the public garden on the rue Magenta: the monument to the dead of the Vienne
stops.date_confidence: the French works list gives the garden, the rue Magenta and the inauguration year 1895; no day is given. The coordinate approximates that garden and is not a surveyed position of the monument
stops.campa: Twenty-five years after the defeat, the department of the Vienne raises a monument to its soldiers killed in the war against Prussia, and the commission travels to Paris and comes back as bronze and stone. It stands in the public garden on the rue Magenta, among provincial gravel walks, a long way from any fairground. Work of this kind, voted by a departmental council, keeps a Paris studio solvent between world's fairs and puts the same grieving figures into a hundred French towns. Nothing records whether he came to see it standing.
suggested_refs: Monument aux soldats de la Vienne morts en 1870, jardin public de la rue Magenta, Poitiers

stops.name: École des beaux-arts: the chair of sculpture
stops.date_confidence: the French sources give the professorship from 1894, on his resignation from Sèvres; the English article gives 1900, which conflates the chair with the academy election of that year, and one French page names him among a pupil's masters as early as 1882. The start year is contested between sources and is left contested
stops.campa: He takes a chair at the school that trained him and teaches from the far side of the atelier for the rest of his working life: Mahmoud Mokhtar out of Egypt, Marcel Gaumont, Raymond Delamarre, Louis Leygue, Hippolyte Lefèbvre, the Argentine Rogelio Yrurtia frequenting the studio. What he teaches is the line that was taught to him. Of Auguste Rodin, refused three times by this school as a boy and by now the most famous sculptor in France, he says one word, fumiste, a joker, not serious, and he says it from a chair Rodin was never allowed to sit beneath.
suggested_refs: The sculpture atelier of the École nationale supérieure des beaux-arts under Coutan

stops.name: Opéra-Comique, salle Favart: ten caryatids inside the house
stops.date_confidence: the date is the opening of Louis Bernier's third salle Favart, attested by the French article on the Opéra-Comique. No date is recorded for the carving of the caryatids themselves; the English article's 1899 is the year after the house opened
stops.campa: The second salle Favart burned in May 1887. The house that replaces it opens on the seventh of December 1898 wearing Denys Puech's Music and Ernest Guilbert's Poetry on its front; his own contribution is indoors, ten caryatids holding up the boxes of the auditorium. Nobody on the boulevard sees them. They are visible for the length of an opera to an audience that has paid to come in, above its own head, in a house where the programme prints the composer, the singers, the conductor, and not the man who carved the women bearing the tiers.
suggested_refs: The ten caryatids of the auditorium, third salle Favart, Opéra-Comique

stops.name: Muséum national d'histoire naturelle: Les Chasseurs d'aigles
stops.date_confidence: the French works list gives a plaster high relief of 1900 and a bronze cast in 1900-1901 on the street facade of the anthropology gallery. The English article's span of 1893-1900, with installation in 1900, is a separate account and is not reconciled here. The coordinate is the museum grounds; the exact facade is not confirmed by any source consulted
stops.campa: Two hunters wrestle eagles on a wall of the natural history museum, muscle against wing, myth pressed into the service of a scientific institution. The bronze is cast for the street front of the anthropology gallery; the plaster it was pulled from goes to the national collections. The Jardin des Plantes is where France keeps its specimens, its skeletons and its argument about the descent of man, and what it puts on the outside wall is a naked man taking a bird by the throat with his hands.
suggested_refs: 'Les Chasseurs d'aigles', bronze, galerie d'anthropologie, Muséum national d'histoire naturelle

stops.name: Musée d'Orsay: the plaster of the eagle hunters
stops.date_confidence: the plaster is dated 1900 by the French works list, which also gives its present home. The museum on the quai d'Orsay opened in 1986, so this stop marks where the object ended, not where it stood in his lifetime. A claim that the plaster was shown at the Salon of 1900 in the new Grand Palais is in no source consulted and is not carried
stops.campa: The plaster stays. Plaster is the sculptor's own hand, the thing he actually modelled; bronze is the foundry's translation of it, stone the carver's. The high relief of the eagle hunters survives in the material he touched, in the national collections, and now hangs in a converted railway station on the quai d'Orsay, a few hundred metres upstream from the bridge where his Renaissance France stands at the foot of a pylon. The station stopped taking trains in 1939, the year he died, and became a museum forty-seven years later.
suggested_refs: 'Les Chasseurs d'aigles', plaster high relief, 1900, musée d'Orsay

stops.name: Square Félix-Desruelles: the portique of the Sèvres pavilion
stops.date_confidence: the portique is attested as made in 1900 for the exposition; no date is given for its re-erection in the square. The coordinate is the square's own, 168 bis boulevard Saint-Germain
stops.campa: For the pavilion of the porcelain works he had directed, at the exposition of 1900, he and the architect Charles-Auguste Risler build a portique in enamelled stoneware: Art Nouveau, glazed, the single object in his whole production that belongs to the new style rather than to the Institut. Fairs are pulled down as a matter of course. This one is not. It is re-erected off the boulevard Saint-Germain beside the oldest church in Paris, and a temporary entrance to a trade display has now stood there for more than a century.
suggested_refs: The portique in grès émaillé, square Félix-Desruelles, Paris 6e
Charles-Auguste Risler (1864-1937), architect, its co-author

stops.name: Pont Alexandre III: La France de la Renaissance
stops.date_confidence: the bridge was built for the exposition of 1900 and the group is attested as his; no separate date is recorded for the group itself
stops.campa: Four Frances sit at the feet of the four pylons of the new bridge, one epoch each: medieval France, the France of the Renaissance, the France of Louis XIV, modern France, with gilded winged figures overhead on the pylon tops. His is the Renaissance, on the upstream pylon of the left bank. The first stone was laid in 1896 by Tsar Nicholas II, for a bridge named after his dead father, in an alliance made of stone and gold leaf. Every figure on the bridge, his included, was commissioned and judged by the institution that gave him the Prix de Rome.
suggested_refs: 'La France de la Renaissance', pylon base, pont Alexandre-III

stops.name: Institut de France, quai de Conti: the seat of Falguière
stops.date_confidence: the election is attested for 1900, on the death of Alexandre Falguière on 19 April of that year, and is given independently by the French and Spanish articles. The English article's 1905 is an error and is not carried. No day of the election is recorded
stops.campa: Alexandre Falguière dies in April and the fourth seat of the sculpture section falls vacant. Coutan is elected into it, under the dome on the quai de Conti where the five academies of France sit, in the same institution that gave him the Prix de Rome twenty-eight years earlier: judged, then judge. He is fifty-one, holds a chair at the school, and has just taken the Grand Prix of the exposition for the Sèvres portique. He will keep the fourth seat for thirty-nine years, until his death.
suggested_refs: Fauteuil 4, section de sculpture, Académie des beaux-arts, in succession to Alexandre Falguière

stops.name: Petit Palais: La Porteuse de pain
stops.date_confidence: undated. The French works list gives the work and the museum and no year and no material; the date here is a placeholder set at the year the Petit Palais was built and is not attested. A description of the piece as a plaster model is likewise unsourced
stops.campa: A woman carrying bread stands in the city's own museum, across the avenue from the Grand Palais. She is not France, not Peace, not Science, not the Renaissance: a working woman under a load, made by the hand that gives gods to railway stations. Academic training begins with bodies and only afterwards puts names on them, and a bread carrier under her load is the same problem as a hunter holding an eagle. Nothing in the record says when he made her, or out of what.
suggested_refs: 'La Porteuse de pain', Petit Palais, musée des Beaux-Arts de la Ville de Paris

stops.name: Pont de Bir-Hakeim: La Science and Le Travail
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The two bas-reliefs are attested on the central arch of the bridge, then the pont de Passy; no source consulted dates them, and 1905 is a placeholder inside the construction window of 1903-1905. The coordinate is the midpoint of the bridge
stops.campa: On the arch that carries the viaduct over the Île aux Cygnes he cuts two reliefs, Science and Labour, for a crossing built to carry the Métro above the road and the road above the river. The bridge is called the pont de Passy while he works on it. After the second war it is renamed for a battle fought in the Libyan desert in 1942, and the two reliefs keep the names they were given in a century that still expected both of those words to be good news.
suggested_refs: 'La Science' and 'Le Travail', bas-reliefs of the central arch, pont de Bir-Hakeim

segments.name: The Ocean the Work Crosses Alone

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the Paz mausoleum
stops.date_confidence: 1904 is the commission year given by the Spanish article on the cemetery; no month is given and no completion date is recorded. The dead man's name is given as José Camilo Paz on one Spanish page and José Clemente Paz on another, and the two are not reconciled here. The coordinate is the cemetery, a single pin for a burial ground of five and a half hectares
stops.campa: The family that owns La Prensa commissions a tomb in the necropolis behind the Franciscan convent, in honour of a son, José Jacobo Gainza Paz. Two white Carrara angels flank a bronze door set in a cubic base of black granite, one of them crowned, one holding an anchor. The father, who founded the newspaper, is laid inside it eight years later. The sculptor is in Paris. The marble is cut there, crated and shipped, and set up by other hands in a burial ground he will never walk through.
suggested_refs: The Paz mausoleum, Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Paris, the atelier: a colleague reports a cast on the shelf
stops.date_confidence: the article carrying the report was published in 1906; the visit it describes is undated, and the studio's address is unknown, so the coordinate remains the reconstructed sculptors' quarter
stops.campa: The archaeologist Maxime Collignon, publishing on a marble head of Eros, mentions in passing where he saw a certain plaster cast: in the studio of his colleague and friend Monsieur Jules Coutan, of the Académie des beaux-arts, who had it directly from Monsieur Bovet in the years he was a pensionnaire in Rome. It is the only look inside that studio in anything reachable. A cast carried home from Italy thirty years before is still standing there, and a member of the Institut is working among such things at the age of fifty-seven.
stops.quote: J'ai vu un de ces moulages dans l'atelier de mon confrère et ami M. Jules Coutan, de l'Académie des Beaux-Arts, qui l'a reçu directement de M. Bovet, au temps où il était pensionnaire de l'Académie de France à la Villa Médicis.
stops.quote_source: Maxime Collignon, 'Tête d'Éros en marbre de la Collection d'Harcourt', Monuments et mémoires de la Fondation Eugène Piot, vol. 13, no. 2 (1906), p. 141, consulted at persee.fr
suggested_refs: Maxime Collignon, 'Tête d'Éros en marbre de la Collection d'Harcourt' (1906)

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the Avellaneda monument
stops.date_confidence: 1910 is the date given by the Spanish source; a brief that grouped this work with the Paz commission of 1904 is a separate account and is not reconciled with it. No month is given
stops.campa: Nicolás Avellaneda, president of Argentina from 1874 to 1880, the man whose government sent the army into Patagonia and took in the peace terms of the Araucanian chiefs, is given a monument executed entirely in Carrara marble: a woman kneeling in prayer beside his carved portrait, three metres high, two and a half wide. It is the second Coutan in this ground. Argentine political money is now buying its funeral sculpture in Paris by name, and the marble travels from Carrara through a Paris workshop to a plot in Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Avellaneda mausoleum, Cementerio de la Recoleta, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Cementerio de la Recoleta: the tomb of General Campos
stops.date_confidence: undated. Two sources, the English article on the cemetery and the Spanish article on Coutan, independently credit him with the Luis María Campos tomb; neither gives a year. The date here is a placeholder set beside the other Recoleta work and is not attested
stops.campa: A third vault in the same walled ground carries his name: General Luis María Campos, soldier of the Paraguayan war and of the frontier, minister of war. No year attaches to it in anything reachable, and no French list of his works mentions it; the attribution comes from two encyclopaedias in two other languages. Three tombs now stand in this walled ground, all cut from models made in a single Paris studio. Nowhere outside Paris holds three of his works inside one enclosure.
suggested_refs: The Luis María Campos mausoleum, Cementerio de la Recoleta

stops.name: Paris, the atelier: the model for Grand Central
stops.date_confidence: the working span is contradicted between sources: Wikidata gives 1907-1913, the English article 1911-1914, for the same commission. Neither is preferred here; the date is the earliest year the English account allows. The studio's location remains a reconstruction
stops.campa: A railway company in New York wants gods over its front door and orders them from a Paris academician. He models Mercury, god of commerce and of travellers, flanked by Minerva and Hercules, at a quarter of the size the facade demands. The model is crated and crosses the Atlantic. In New York the John Donnelly Company enlarges it and cuts the stone, so the surface over Forty-second Street is Donnelly's hand working to a French plaster, and the man who shaped that plaster is at his bench in Paris the whole time.
suggested_refs: The John Donnelly Company, New York, carvers of the Grand Central group

stops.name: Grand Central Terminal, 42nd Street: the group unveiled
stops.date_confidence: the year of the unveiling is attested; no source consulted gives the day. A New York Times article of 14 June 1914 announced the group, and only its headline could be verified: the newspaper's own archive was unreachable from this environment, so the body of that article is not quoted
stops.campa: Forty-eight feet high, sixty-six feet wide, some fifteen hundred tons of stone: Mercury above the clock, Minerva and Hercules at his sides, called at the unveiling the largest sculptural group in the world. Below it a thirteen-foot clock is set into the façade, and below that the traffic of a continent goes in and out of a terminal built to swallow it. The man who designed the group is sixty-five years old and in Paris. He does not come to the unveiling. He never in his life sets foot in the United States.
stops.quote: WORLD'S LARGEST SCULPTURE GROUP FOR NEW YORK; Figures for Grand Central Station Are 50 Feet High
stops.quote_source: The New York Times, 14 June 1914, headline only; the article text could not be fetched, timesmachine.nytimes.com being blocked from this environment
suggested_refs: 'Glory of Commerce', Grand Central Terminal, 42nd Street facade

stops.name: Plaza Carlos Pellegrini, Buenos Aires: the monument in Carrara marble
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by the Spanish sources; no day is recorded. Two pins for this plaza circulate in the working material, some 350 metres apart and both south of the site; the coordinate here is the head of the avenida Alvear near Cerrito and Arroyo
stops.campa: At the head of the avenida Alvear, in Carrara marble and bronze, Carlos Pellegrini stands surrounded by figures of the Republic, of justice, of progress. He was president of Argentina for two years, put into the office by a revolution he did not lead, and he founded the bank that still carries the state's money. The monument goes up in 1914, the same year Mercury is raised over Forty-second Street. He is sixty-five years old, at his bench in Paris, and neither of the two unveilings has him at it.
suggested_refs: The monument to Carlos Pellegrini, Plaza Carlos Pellegrini, Retiro, Buenos Aires

stops.name: Paris, sixth arrondissement: the death at ninety
stops.date_confidence: attested by the French and English articles. The address within the sixth arrondissement is not recorded and the coordinate is the district
stops.campa: He dies at ninety in the sixth arrondissement, a few streets from the school where he was trained and where he taught. The world that commissioned him has gone ahead of him: the expositions dismantled, the departmental memorials weathering, the Republic no longer wanting its bridges to argue in allegory. Auguste Rodin, whom this school refused three times and whom he called a joker, has been dead twenty-two years and took the century's taste with him. Six months after the funeral, Germany invades Poland.
suggested_refs: The death notice of Jules Coutan, February 1939

stops.name: Cimetière de Montmartre: division 25
stops.date_confidence: the burial date and the division are attested by the French article. The coordinate is the centre of the cemetery; the plot is not located in any source consulted, and two other pins for this grave circulate in the working material, both outside the cemetery walls
stops.campa: Two days later he is put into the twenty-fifth division of the Montmartre cemetery, under the road viaduct, among writers and singers and painters. Nothing of his own scale marks him. Fifteen metres of stone gods stand over a railway station in New York, two marble angels over a newspaperman's vault in Buenos Aires, four Frances at the pylons of a gilded bridge a half hour's walk from here, and the man who modelled all of it lies under a slab in the only one of those places he could ever reach on foot.
suggested_refs: The grave of Jules Coutan, 25th division, cimetière de Montmartre

stops.name: Palais des Académies, Brussels: the death entered in the minutes
stops.date_confidence: attested: the session of Thursday 2 March 1939 of the Classe des Beaux-Arts of the Académie royale de Belgique, printed in its Bulletin, volume 21 (1939), pages 51-52. No source consulted records any visit by Coutan to Belgium
stops.campa: In Brussels, at the session of the second of March, the president reports the death of Monsieur Jules Coutan, associate of the sculpture section since 1920, and expresses the regret his loss causes the academy. Nineteen years of foreign membership are closed in one sentence and entered in a bulletin. Academies keep their dead this way, in the minutes, between the reading of the correspondence and the next item of business, and this one keeps him in a city he is nowhere recorded as having visited.
stops.quote: M. le Président fait part du décès de M. Jules Coutan, associé de la Section de Sculpture depuis 1920, et exprime les regrets que cause à l'Académie la perte de ce distingué Confrère.
